strengths: Addresses a genuine research gap with a comprehensive benchmark for GUI-shortcut hybrid mobile agents, filling an important evaluation gap in the field
Novel evaluation framework for assessing agent-generated shortcuts using standardized baseline, enabling unbiased quality assessment of different generation strategies
Well-designed benchmark with 139 complex tasks across 11 real-world apps, diverse shortcut types (APIs, deep-links, RPA), and thoughtfully incomplete knowledge bases that test planning and reasoning
Multi-dimensional evaluation metrics capturing success rate, efficiency (MS, MSR, MET), and cost dimensions (MToC, MSC, SSR, GSAR) with strong motivation for each

Strong experimental results demonstrating clear benefits of hybrid approaches (64.1% vs 44.6% SR), framework-agnostic applicability across different UI representations, and greater benefits for weaker models
Comprehensive documentation with detailed appendices, standardized emulator environment, and error case analysis supporting reproducibility
Honest reporting of limitations, including the significant underperformance of agent-generated shortcuts compared to predefined ones
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—proposed agents (MAS-MobileAgent, MAS-T3A) simply inject shortcuts into prompts without novel selection, planning, or ranking mechanisms for intelligent shortcut utilization

Agent-generated shortcuts substantially underperform predefined ones (34-49% vs 52% SR), with dynamic shortcuts achieving 38% SR worse than baseline (43%), undermining the primary motivation for the generation evaluation framework and raising questions about practical utility

Narrow experimental scope with only four baseline agents (T3A, M3A, MobileAgentV2, MobileAgent-E) and limited exploration of diverse shortcut selection strategies; Gemini-2.0-Flash only briefly evaluated despite motivation from weaker-model scenarios

Shortcut knowledge base construction relies on manual curation with unclear scalability—11 apps and 88 shortcuts lack justification for representativeness; no discussion of maintenance or adaptation as apps evolve

Shortcut generation evaluation uses only 50% of tasks without justification; unclear if subset is representative; relatively small number of generated shortcuts per type (36-46) limits statistical reliability
Limited analysis of why agent-generated shortcuts fail and how to improve robustness; error analysis in Appendix D remains superficial without proposed solutions
Task design and knowledge base incompleteness may not reflect realistic agent scenarios; limited analysis of task representativeness relative to actual mobile usage patterns

Scope limited to mobile domain with unclear generalization to web, desktop, or other platforms; primarily a systems paper with limited relevance to core NLP research, potentially better suited for AI/ML venues
No mention of code/data availability or release plans; full reproduction requires access to real Android apps and internals; dependency on specific emulator setup could hinder reproduction
Insufficient investigation into root causes of poor agent-generated shortcut performance and missing discussion of potential solutions or alternative generation approaches

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap in systematic evaluation of GUI-shortcut hybrid mobile agents with a well-designed, comprehensive benchmark (139 tasks, 88 shortcuts, 7 metrics)
Novel two-stage evaluation framework for agent-generated shortcuts with diverse generation strategies (task replay, subtask replay, dynamic, MobileAgent-E)
Demonstrates framework-agnostic applicability by testing on both visual and UI-tree-based agents (MAS-MobileAgent and MAS-T3A)
Clear empirical validation that hybrid agents significantly outperform GUI-only baselines (64.1% vs 44.6% success rate), with thorough analysis showing greater benefits for weaker models
Comprehensive experimental analysis including bad case categorization (selection/planning errors, behavioral/adaptation errors, execution errors) providing actionable insights
weaknesses: Limited novelty—primarily an engineering/benchmarking contribution without algorithmic innovation in how agents should recognize, select, or compose shortcuts. Proposed agents (MAS-MobileAgent, MAS-T3A) are straightforward prompt-injection baselines

Agent-generated shortcuts underperform significantly (Replay-Task: 34% SR with 10% SSR; Dynamic: 38% SR; Replay-Subtask: 43% SR showing no improvement), undermining the core motivation for evaluating shortcut generation and raising questions about viability

Questionable soundness of shortcut generation evaluation: using a single baseline agent (T3A) to evaluate all generated shortcuts may unfairly disadvantage shortcuts optimized for different agent architectures; inconsistent task subset (50% for generation vs. 100% for main evaluation) raises reproducibility concerns

Narrow baseline comparisons (only 3 GUI-only agents + 1 self-evolved agent); acknowledged limitation of underexplored baselines; no evaluation of concurrent hybrid approaches (UFO2, AppAgentX) on the same benchmark despite citing them

Limited benchmark coverage and scalability: only 11 apps with uneven shortcut distribution (Fitbit: 21, Calendar: 2); manually curated KB lacks clear methodology for systematic expansion; no validation that 139 tasks represent real user needs

Incomplete analysis of key phenomena: why shortcuts help weak models more (empirically shown but not deeply investigated); which task types benefit most; why generated shortcuts have low SSR (e.g., 10% for Replay-Task)—insufficient investigation of failure mechanisms

Methodological concerns: no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or reported run variance; GSAR metric interpretation ambiguous; dramatic SSR range (10%-100%) suggests robustness issues not thoroughly addressed

Reproducibility gaps: prompt engineering details sparse; automated evaluation methodology incompletely specified; 'project page available at [URL]' with actual URL missing; no code/data release mentioned
Limited scope and generalization: Android-only (narrow mobile definition); only Gemini models tested; results may not generalize to other LLMs (GPT-4, Claude) or rapidly evolving model capabilities

Limited practical utility: gap between predefined (100% SSR) and agent-generated shortcuts (10%-75% SSR) suggests latter not production-ready; insufficient guidance for practitioners on when/how to use benchmark or implications for future agent design

strengths: Addresses a clear and timely gap: first benchmark specifically designed to evaluate GUI-shortcut hybrid mobile agents, filling a documented need in the rapidly growing field of LLM-based mobile automation

Comprehensive and well-designed benchmark: 139 real-world tasks across 11 apps, 88 predefined shortcuts (APIs, deep links, RPA scripts), 7 multi-dimensional evaluation metrics, with careful task categorization (single-app and cross-app)

Novel shortcut generation evaluation framework: Two-stage methodology using a unified baseline agent isolates shortcut quality from agent-specific capabilities, enabling unbiased assessment of generation strategies

Strong empirical validation with clear results: 64.1% vs 44.6% success rate improvement, 40% efficiency gain, tested across different agent architectures (screenshot and UI-tree) and model capabilities
Insightful finding on model capability: Demonstrates that weaker models (Gemini 2.0-Flash) benefit substantially more from shortcuts than stronger ones, with practical implications
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed environment specifications, comprehensive appendices, action space definitions, and promised code/data release
Thorough failure analysis: Categorization of error types (planning, adaptation, formulation) provides useful insights into agent limitations beyond aggregate metrics
weaknesses: Severely limited baseline comparisons: Only 3 GUI-only agents and 1 self-generated shortcut method evaluated; insufficient to validate whether the benchmark effectively discriminates between hybrid strategies or merely confirms that shortcuts help (an expected result)

Agent-generated shortcut framework significantly underperforms, raising fundamental questions: Only 52% SR for predefined vs 43-38% for generated shortcuts; Replay-Task only 10% SSR; no analysis of whether generation methods or evaluation framework is flawed

Critical design choice under-justified: Knowledge base intentionally incomplete but principles and extent of incompleteness not specified; no ablation study; unclear if this design biases results toward overstating shortcut benefits

Insufficient analysis of when/why shortcuts help: No task categorization by benefit magnitude; missing correlation analysis between task characteristics and shortcut effectiveness; cross-app underperformance (61.7% vs 64.1%) not analyzed

Underspecified methodological details: Shortcut retrieval mechanism not clearly described; MSR metric using 'optimal steps' appears subjective; 50% subset for generation evaluation not justified; no statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals
Narrow scope limits generalizability: Android-only, 11 apps, mobile domain-specific; results may not transfer beyond these contexts; only 7 RPA scripts across 11 apps appears sparse

Dynamic shortcuts concerning finding buried: These show 38% success (worse than 43% baseline) despite high efficiency claim; insufficient analysis of this troubling result and its implications for future research
Venue appropriateness concern: While benchmark papers are accepted at ACL, this is primarily a systems/applications contribution with limited core NLP/computational linguistics novelty

strengths: Well-designed and comprehensive benchmark addressing a clear gap in GUI-shortcut hybrid agent evaluation, with 139 tasks across 11 apps and thoughtful categorization
Rigorous reproducibility through snapshot-based reset mechanism, dedicated test accounts, and detailed environment specifications enabling fair comparison
Innovative automated evaluation pipeline (MAS-Bench-Eval) with high human agreement (F1=96.3%, Precision=98.1%) using elegant two-stage Describe-and-Judge framework

Extensive experimental validation across diverse agent architectures (agentic workflows, general-purpose models, specialized GUI models) revealing nuanced findings about model-capability-dependent shortcut effectiveness

Strong analysis of amplified benefits on cross-app tasks (263% SR improvement) and identification of shortcut misuse robustness through interference testing, demonstrating benchmark's discriminative power
Excellent documentation and reproducibility with clear methodology for human baselines, detailed environment specification, and transparent shortcut collection/design process
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty—primarily an engineering contribution; shortcut retrieval is simplistic keyword-based matching, injection is straightforward prompt augmentation, and evaluation metrics are largely standard

Critical unresolved problem: Agent-generated shortcuts catastrophically fail (Replay-Task 10% SSR, best method 49% vs 52% baseline), significantly undermining the stated contribution of evaluating shortcut generation capabilities with no proposed solutions

Unrealistic shortcut discovery assumption—keyword-based retrieval with app-name filtering explicitly 'isolates shortcut selection from open-domain retrieval failures' (stated limitation); real agents must discover shortcuts, a fundamental challenge not addressed

Limited scope and scalability: only 11 consumer apps, 139 tasks (modest for modern benchmarks), mobile-only generalizability unclear, manually-curated knowledge base doesn't scale, no maintenance/versioning strategy discussed

Insufficient analysis of shortcut generation: evaluation uses only 50% of tasks, reasons for catastrophic failure (10% SSR) unexplored, minimal exploration of alternatives to action replay, no concrete recommendations beyond identifying as future work

Statistical rigor absent—no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance analysis reported; appears to be single runs; power may be limited with task subsampling (69 of 139 for shortcut evaluation)

Agent architecture design underexplored: MAS-MobileAgent/MAS-T3A are trivial prompt augmentations; no ablation studies on retrieval strategies, injection methods, or shortcut representations; missed opportunity to investigate optimal integration approaches
Shortcut stability claims lack evidence—testing 'across at least five versions' mentioned in Appendix A.4 but with no quantitative data or robustness metrics supporting stability claims
Benchmark sustainability unclear—no discussion of app update maintenance strategy, emulator snapshot brittleness with versions, or community extensibility plans for long-term viability

Missing analysis of specialized GUI model underperformance: ScaleCUA/others don't benefit from shortcuts despite general-purpose models doing so; underlying causes not investigated; deserves deeper exploration
